1:
The heading names an occasion, and the first difficulty is a name inside it. Augustine of Hippo observes that the title calls the priest Abimelech whereas the history calls him Achimelech, and that one might suppose the similarity of the names and the difference of a single letter had confused them; but he reports that the manuscripts he examined read the first form, and he points to another psalm whose title names the same man where the history has a wholly different king. From this he draws a rule rather than a correction: the very change of name should make us the more intent upon a mystery, so that we do not pursue the apparent facts of history and despise the sacred veilings. Keil and Delitzsch defend the headings generally, counting this among eight psalms whose inscriptions assign them to the persecution by Saul, some of which can be verified and none of which can be replaced by anything more credible; they note in passing that Augustine had a name for that group. Adam Clarke reports that all the versions agree with this title except one, which takes the psalm for an attack on vice in general, and then enters a dissent of his own: granting it is plainly an invective against some great and tyrannical man, he thinks it too mild in composition for a transaction that is the most barbarous on record.

Whom it addresses is less settled than the title suggests. Matthew Henry, John Calvin and John Gill all take the informer, whom Henry describes as mighty by office, set over the household. C.H. Spurgeon raises the possibility that the words are aimed past him at the king, in which case they are spoken pityingly, asking how one fitted by nature for nobler deeds could descend to find a theme for boasting in so heartless a slaughter. On the title given him they converge, all hearing sarcasm. Charles Ellicott says the word is better rendered hero and used sarcastically, though he rejects on grammatical grounds the older versions that make him a hero at mischief. John Wesley supplies the tone: O valiant captain, to kill a few weak and unarmed persons. Spurgeon says honourable titles are but irony where the wearer is mean and cruel, since it took no might to kill men who never touched a sword. Henry puts it best of the four: it is no honour for those that wear a sword to hector those that wear an ephod.

The figure of the razor is read the same two ways by two of them. Clarke says the instrument that should take off the beard instead cuts and wounds the flesh, or the operator who pretends to trim it cuts the throat; Spurgeon offers the barber who makes a man bald before he notices, so softly and deftly is the work done, or the throat cut speedily under the pretence of shaving. Clarke then itemises the character in seven counts, from boasting in the power to do evil down to a tongue that pretended friendship while the heart was full of enmity, and turns to the punishment. Ellicott glosses the devouring words as words that swallow down a neighbour’s life, honour and goods, and Spurgeon likens them to constrictors that swallow men whole. Gill reads the whole description forward as a prophecy of antichrist, boasting of merit and of works of supererogation and of blood shed in what was thought to be God’s service. Calvin explains the term in the heading as marking psalms in which David records being chastised or admonished, the affliction sent like a schoolmaster’s rod.
5:
The verbs of the sentence are taken apart word by word. Adam Clarke distributes them into three acts: God will pull down the building, unroof it, dilapidate it and dig up its foundation; he will break the man to pieces so that he has neither strength nor support; and he will mow him down and sweep him away like chaff in a whirlwind, so that he has no residence and no tent left. Charles Ellicott fixes on the second verb, which he renders lay hold of and which is always used of taking a live coal from the hearth; and he notes that exactly the opposite of our own phrase about plucking a brand from the burning is intended here, since the idea is of pulling the house-fire to pieces and so extinguishing domestic life. John Gill observes that the first word is used of breaking down a house infected with leprosy, and takes it of the utter extinction of the informer’s family. John Wesley presses the suddenness and the completeness, that though the man seems to have taken deep root he shall be plucked up by the very roots. Ellicott and Keil and Delitzsch both hear the uprooting as set against the tree of the following verse, the betrayer becoming an uprooted tree while the betrayed stands like a green olive planted in sacred and inaccessible ground.

What the righteous feel when they see it is a textual question as well as a moral one. Clarke reports that three manuscripts and one ancient version read they shall rejoice where the received text has they shall fear, and holds this the true reading, since laughter follows immediately and is the natural companion of rejoicing rather than of dread. The others defend the harder text and find the tension in it deliberate. Ellicott says the mingled feelings of awe at the tyrant’s terrible fall and exultation at his overthrow are finely caught and described. Wesley glosses the fear as reverence for a just judgment, and Matthew Henry makes it awe at the justice of God before whom the proudest sinner cannot stand. C.H. Spurgeon keeps both, holy awe sobering the mind and then laughter, if not of righteous joy then of solemn contempt at schemes so far-reaching all baffled. Henry insists the laughter is not ludicrous but rational and serious, and adds a guard: lest the triumph should look like personal revenge, the psalmist does not speak of it as his own act but puts it in the mouth of other righteous persons.

The epitaph on the fallen man draws the sharpest moral in the chapter, and it is about money. Gill contrasts those who make God their strong hold, running thither and being safe, with the rich man whose wealth is his strong city. Spurgeon says wealth and wickedness are dreadful companions which combined make a monster, and that when the devil is master of the money bags he is a devil indeed. Clarke goes furthest. Quoting a Latin line to the effect that the love of money grows exactly as the money grows, he asks where the religious man is in whose hands money has multiplied and who has not lost the spirit of piety in the same proportion; and he says there is no way to prevent this, and the perdition it leads to, but opening both hands to the poor. Henry observes only that the fall of a wealthy and mighty man cannot but be generally noticed, and that the remark the righteous should make on it is the one the psalm supplies.
8:
Two of them change the tense before they begin. John Gill holds that the words should be supplied as I shall be, since the speaker was at that moment an exile from the house of God, so that the line is a confidence rather than a description; Adam Clarke renders it the same way. On the tree itself Gill assembles its properties: a choice and fruitful tree with fatness in it, producing excellent oil, delighting in hot climates and sunny places, found on mountains, evergreen and durable, its leaves and branches symbols of peace. Charles Ellicott corrects one of these. The epithet rendered green, he says, hardly refers to colour so much as to vigour, since the foliage of the olive cannot be called verdant; and though the tree is scarcely a beautiful one to Western eyes, he quotes a naturalist for whom the coolness of its pale foliage and its evergreen freshness, spread like a silver sea along the slopes of the hills, speak of peace and plenty and gladness. He adds that the olive alternates with the vine in Hebrew poetry as an emblem of a prosperous nation.

Whether anything was actually planted there divides them flatly. Clarke states as a matter of course that it does not mean there were olive trees planted in God’s house, only that the man was there as the olive is in its proper soil and situation. Ellicott holds the opposite possible: trees may really have stood in the precincts of the temple, as they do in the same enclosure now, so that a rendering near the house of God would state a literal fact; though he allows that the whole may equally be figurative. Keil and Delitzsch take the location as the point of the figure whichever way it is read, the betrayed man standing planted in ground that is sacred and inaccessible while the betrayer is torn up. Clarke sets the two trees against each other directly: the one bringing forth poisonous fruit is cursed and pulled up from the roots, the other in good soil bears fruit to God’s glory and stays green.

The bare clause of the last verse, that God has done it, is filled in three ways. Keil and Delitzsch refer it to the gracious and just carrying out of what was aimed at in the choice of David. John Wesley makes it concrete and future, the destruction of the enemies and the establishing of the speaker on the throne, of which he says he is no less assured than if it were already done. Clarke keeps it general, that all his good comes from God and is therefore the ground of praise. On the waiting that follows, Clarke turns it into a practice rather than a posture: he will expect the continuation of the blessings by uniting with the saints in using the ordinances, and that, he says, is how he will wait.
